seo.title: Engine Warranty Claim Guide | Step-by-Step UK Process
seo.description: Follow our step-by-step guide to make an engine warranty claim. Learn what documents you need, your legal rights, and what to do if a supplier refuses a valid claim.

hero.title: What to do if something goes wrong

content.text: If your replacement engine develops a problem within the warranty period, the first and most important step is to contact the supplier who sold you the engine - not us. This guide walks you through the entire process.

Engines Market does not mediate disputes - but we do track complaints to keep our network accountable. This guide explains how to make a warranty claim, what documentation you’ll need, what to do if the supplier is unresponsive, and your legal rights.

1-contact-the-supplier-first.title: 1 Contact the supplier first
1-contact-the-supplier-first.description: Always start with the supplier who provided the engine. They are responsible for honouring the warranty. Do not take the car to another garage for repair without speaking to the supplier first - they may need to inspect the engine themselves, and unauthorised work can void the warranty.

content.text: What to say when you call or email:

items: “I bought a [reconditioned / used / rebuilt] engine from you on [date]. My invoice number is [XXX].”
“It has developed the following problem: [describe symptoms - noise, smoke, loss of power, warning lights].”
“I believe this should be covered under the warranty. Please advise on next steps.”

content.text: Keep a record of every call (time, date, who you spoke to) and save all emails.

2-gather-your-documentation.title: 2 Gather your documentation
2-gather-your-documentation.description: Before you contact the supplier, collect these documents. They will ask for them.

rows: Original invoice
Proves purchase date, engine type, and warranty start date
Warranty document
Shows what is covered (parts only or parts and labour) and exclusions
Photos or videos of the problem
Visual evidence of smoke, leaks, noises, warning lights
Fault codes (if available)
If a garage has scanned the ECU, get the codes
Service records
Oil change receipts, maintenance logs - prove you followed the supplier’s requirements
Mileage at installation and now
Shows how many miles you have driven under warranty

content.text: If you do not have something, explain why. Missing service records are a common reason claims are rejected.

3-give-the-supplier-a-reasonable-chance-.title: 3 Give the supplier a reasonable chance to respond
3-give-the-supplier-a-reasonable-chance-.description: Most suppliers will respond within a few working days. If they ask you to bring the vehicle to them or to an approved garage for inspection, cooperate.

items: Claim approved - Supplier arranges a replacement engine and (if covered) the labour to fit it. You may need to pay for consumables (oil, coolant, gaskets).
Claim declined - Supplier explains why (e.g., “installation error”, “neglect”, “excluded part”). Ask for the reason in writing.
No response - If the supplier ignores you after repeated attempts, move to Step 4.

4-if-the-supplier-is-unresponsive-or-ref.title: 4 If the supplier is unresponsive or refuses a valid claim
4-if-the-supplier-is-unresponsive-or-ref.description: You have options - but Engines Market does not mediate or enforce warranty terms.

content.text: We do not get involved in individual disputes. However, we do track complaints as part of our supplier monitoring process.
If you believe the supplier has acted unfairly, you can send a copy of your complaint to our monitoring address: complaints@enginesmarket.co.uk

items: Your full name and contact details
The supplier’s name
Invoice number and date of purchase
A summary of the problem and your attempts to resolve it with the supplier
Any supporting documents (invoices, emails, photos)

content.text: What we will do with this information:

items: Log the complaint in our supplier performance records
If we receive multiple similar complaints about the same supplier, we will investigate
If a supplier’s average review rating falls below 3.5 stars (sustained) or they repeatedly fail to honour valid warranties, we may remove them from our network
Mediate between you and the supplier
Demand the supplier accepts your claim
Provide legal advice
Accept liability for the supplier’s warranty

content.text: You should not rely on Engines Market to resolve your dispute. We are a comparison platform, not a warranty administrator.

5-your-legal-rights-and-independent-esca.title: 5 Your legal rights and independent escalation
5-your-legal-rights-and-independent-esca.description: If the supplier refuses a valid claim and you believe you are entitled to a repair, replacement, or refund, you have legal options.

items: Goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, and as described.
If an engine fails within the first 30 days , you can reject it and ask for a full refund.
Within the first six months , the supplier must prove the fault was not present at the time of sale - otherwise, you are entitled to a repair or replacement.
After six months, you may need to prove the fault existed at the time of sale (harder, but not impossible).

rows: Citizens Advice
Free legal guidance on consumer rights
0808 223 1133 / citizensadvice.org.uk
Motor Ombudsman
Independent dispute resolution for the automotive sector (if the supplier is accredited)
themotorombudsman.org
Small claims court
Legal route for claims up to £10,000 - relatively low cost, no solicitor required
gov.uk/make-court-claim-for-money

content.text: We recommend starting with Citizens Advice. They will help you understand your rights and the best next step.

common-warranty-disputes-and-how-to-avoi.title: Common warranty disputes - and how to avoid them

rows: “The labour to refit is not covered”
Parts-only warranty - common on used engines
Ask before you buy: “Does your warranty cover labour to remove and refit a faulty engine-” Get it in writing.
“The head gasket is excluded”
Gaskets and seals are almost never covered as standalone failures
Ask for a written list of exclusions. If you need a part that is excluded, budget for it.
“You used the wrong oil”
Supplier specified a grade (e.g., 5W-30) but you used something else
Keep receipts for oil and filters. Follow the supplier’s exact recommendations.
“You ignored the warning lights”
Driving with a known problem voids the warranty
Stop driving immediately if you hear noises or see warning lights. Call the supplier before driving further.
“The installation was faulty”
Supplier blames the fitting garage; fitting garage blames the engine
If possible, use a garage approved by the supplier. Keep detailed fitting records and photos.
“The turbo / DPF was damaged by the failed engine”
Consequential damage is almost always excluded
Ask about consequential damage before you buy. If it is excluded (it usually is), accept that risk or buy a more comprehensive warranty elsewhere.

summary-print-this-or-save-it-for-refere.title: Summary - print this or save it for reference

items: Stop driving - If you suspect a problem, stop immediately to avoid voiding the warranty.
Contact the supplier first - Call or email. Keep records.
Gather documentation - Invoice, warranty, photos, fault codes, service records.
Cooperate with inspection - Let the supplier or their approved garage examine the engine.
If approved - Follow their instructions for replacement.
If declined or ignored - Ask for the reason in writing. Then decide: accept the decision, escalate to Citizens Advice or the Motor Ombudsman, or consider small claims court.
Inform Engines Market (for monitoring only) - Send details to complaints@enginesmarket.co.uk so we can track supplier performance.
